concepts.name: Causes and Background of the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782)
key_dimensions: Treaty of Surat (1775): terms, signatories, and why it was controversial within British India (Bombay vs. Calcutta Council conflict)
Succession dispute between Raghunathrao (Raghoba) and Narayan Rao's posthumous heir — Sawai Madhavrao
Role of the Nana Phadnavis and the Pune Darbar in resisting British intervention
Conflict between the Bombay Presidency's unilateral action and the Bengal Council under Warren Hastings — a classic UPSC trap on intra-British authority

concepts.name: Treaty of Surat (1775) vs. Treaty of Purandar (1776): Contrast and Reversal
key_dimensions: Treaty of Surat: signed by Bombay Council with Raghoba, ceding Salsette and Bassein to the British
Treaty of Purandar: Bengal Council's attempt to nullify Surat — terms and why it failed in implementation
Significance of the contradiction between two British presidencies as a structural weakness of early British India governance
UPSC trap: distinguishing which treaty was repudiated and by whom

concepts.name: Convention of Wadgaon (1779): Britain's Humiliation
key_dimensions: Military context: Colonel Cockburn's defeat and the circumstances forcing the Bombay army to capitulate
Key terms: British agreement to restore all conquests since 1773 and surrender of hostages
Warren Hastings's refusal to ratify Wadgaon — significance for understanding British treaty-making authority
UPSC angle: Only major instance of a formal British capitulation to an Indian power in this era — frequently tested as an exception

concepts.name: Treaty of Salbai (1782): Terms, Significance, and 'Status Quo' Principle
key_dimensions: Key terms: restoration of territories, British recognition of Madhavrao II as Peshwa, Raghoba pensioned off
20-year peace clause and its strategic impact on British consolidation in the Deccan
Role of Mahadji Scindia as mediator — his diplomatic rise and British acknowledgment
Contrast with Wadgaon: Salbai restored British prestige; UPSC trap on which party 'won' the First War diplomatically

concepts.name: Nana Phadnavis: Role Across All Three Anglo-Maratha Wars
key_dimensions: His role as de facto regent and diplomat during the First War — architect of Maratha coalition resistance
Drafting and managing the Treaty of Salbai negotiations
Decline of Maratha unity after his death (1800) and its direct link to the Second War
UPSC trap: Often confused with Peshwa; he was the minister (Amatya), not the Peshwa — his title and role must be precise

concepts.name: Causes of the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805): Subsidiary Alliance and Internal Maratha Strife
key_dimensions: Battle of Khadki/Poona (1802): Yashwantrao Holkar's defeat of the Peshwa Baji Rao II
Treaty of Bassein (1802): Baji Rao II accepts subsidiary alliance — significance as the trigger for the Second War
Opposition of Scindia and Bhonsle to the Treaty of Bassein — their perception of British encirclement
Lord Wellesley's 'Ring-fence' policy and subsidiary alliance system as structural causes

concepts.name: Treaty of Bassein (1802): Terms, Implications, and Maratha Reaction
key_dimensions: Key terms: British troops stationed in Pune, Peshwa surrenders foreign policy autonomy, cedes territories for maintenance
Why it was called a 'death warrant of Maratha independence' by historians
Scindia and Bhonsle's refusal to recognize it — direct cause of Second War
UPSC trap: Bassein was signed with the Peshwa (head of Maratha Confederacy), not an individual chief — its confederacy-wide implications

concepts.name: Key Battles of the Second Anglo-Maratha War: Assaye, Laswari, and Argaon
key_dimensions: Battle of Assaye (1803): Arthur Wellesley vs. Scindia and Bhonsle — described by Wellesley as his finest battle
Battle of Laswari (1803): Lake vs. Scindia's forces in the north — strategic significance for Delhi and Agra
Battle of Argaon (1803): defeat of Bhonsle and its role in the Treaty of Deogaon
UPSC angle: Two-front war (Deccan under Arthur Wellesley; Hindustan under Lake) — matching generals to theaters is a frequent trap

concepts.name: Treaties Ending the Second Anglo-Maratha War: Deogaon, Surji-Anjangaon, and Rajpurghat
key_dimensions: Treaty of Deogaon (1803): Bhonsle cedes Cuttack (Odisha) and part of Berar — significance for British control of eastern India
Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803): Scindia cedes Delhi, Agra, Broach, Ahmadnagar; British become protectors of Mughal Emperor
Treaty of Rajpurghat (1803): Holkar's subsidiary terms (though he resumed war)
UPSC trap: Cuttack ceded by Bhonsle, not Scindia — territorial attribution errors are commonly tested

concepts.name: Yashwantrao Holkar and the Holkar Phase of the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1804–1805)
key_dimensions: Holkar's guerrilla warfare strategy and Lake's failed pursuit — demonstrates limits of British conventional warfare
Siege of Bharatpur (1805): British failure against Ranjit Singh Gujar — another rare British setback
Treaty of Rajpurghat (1806): Holkar retains most territories — relatively favorable outcome for Holkar
Recall of Lord Wellesley and policy reversal under Cornwallis — UPSC trap on why the Second War ended inconclusively for Holkar

concepts.name: Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance System: Application to Maratha Chiefs
key_dimensions: Core terms of the subsidiary alliance: British troops, no independent foreign relations, cession of territory for maintenance
Sequential application: Peshwa (Bassein 1802), Bhonsle (Deogaon 1803), Scindia (Surji-Anjangaon 1803)
Holkar's unique resistance and delayed/partial incorporation
UPSC trap: Not all Maratha chiefs accepted simultaneously; order and terms differed — testing sequence and completeness

concepts.name: Causes of the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818): Pindari Connection and British Paramountcy
key_dimensions: Pindari menace: who were Pindaris, their connection to Maratha chiefs (especially Scindia and Holkar as protectors)
Lord Hastings's 'Encircling Movement' (1817) to suppress Pindaris — why it inevitably targeted Maratha chiefs
Baji Rao II's opportunistic attack on the British Residency at Pune (Khadki, 1817) as immediate cause
Treaty of Gwalior (1817) with Scindia — getting Scindia to disown Pindaris before the war

concepts.name: Key Events of the Third Anglo-Maratha War: Khadki, Sitabaldi, Mahidpur
key_dimensions: Battle of Khadki (1817): Baji Rao II attacks British Residency; marks official start of Third War
Battle of Sitabaldi (1817): Bhonsle's forces vs. British at Nagpur — Bhonsle's defeat and submission
Battle of Mahidpur (1817): Holkar's decisive defeat by Malcolm — effectively ends Holkar resistance
UPSC trap: Matching each battle to the correct Maratha chief and British commander is a standard MCQ format

concepts.name: Treaties Ending the Third Anglo-Maratha War: Mandasor, Nagpur, and the Abolition of the Peshwaship
key_dimensions: Treaty of Mandasor (1818): Holkar accepts subsidiary alliance on strict terms
Treaty with Bhonsle of Nagpur: Berar cessions formalized, Nagpur becomes a dependent state
Abolition of the Peshwaship (1818): Baji Rao II surrenders, pensioned off at Bithur (near Kanpur) — end of Maratha political power
UPSC trap: Baji Rao II's pension and residence at Bithur is significant for 1857 (Nana Saheb connection) — cross-topic linkage

concepts.name: Role of Mahadji Scindia in Anglo-Maratha Relations (Pre-Second War)
key_dimensions: His role as mediator in Treaty of Salbai (1782) and rise as the most powerful Maratha chief
Control over the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II — Scindia as 'Deputy Regent of the Mughal Empire'
His death (1794) and its impact on Maratha unity and ability to resist British expansion
UPSC angle: Scindia's dual role — simultaneously cooperating with and restraining British ambitions in north India

concepts.name: Baji Rao II: Character, Policy Failures, and Historical Controversy
key_dimensions: His dependency on British support via Treaty of Bassein — why historians debate whether he had any real alternative
Policy of playing Maratha chiefs against each other (Scindia vs. Holkar) — weakening confederacy from within
His attack at Khadki (1817) as a miscalculation — assessing whether it was opportunism or desperation
UPSC trap: He was the last Peshwa, not the last Maratha ruler — distinction between Peshwaship and other Maratha states

concepts.name: Fragmentation of the Maratha Confederacy as a Structural Cause of British Victory
key_dimensions: The five chief houses: Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaikwad — their mutual rivalries and failure to unite
British strategy of fighting each chief separately rather than facing a unified Maratha force
Contrast with Shivaji's centralized empire — how decentralization enabled British divide-and-rule
UPSC angle: Why the Marathas, despite numerical strength, could not replicate their 18th-century dominance — a synthesis question

concepts.name: Comparison of the Three Anglo-Maratha Wars: Causes, Outcomes, and British Governors-General
key_dimensions: First War (1775–82): Warren Hastings — inconclusive, status quo via Salbai; British internal divisions exposed
Second War (1803–05): Lord Wellesley — decisive British gains (Delhi, Agra, Cuttack); Wellesley recalled for overreach
Third War (1817–18): Lord Hastings — final destruction of Maratha power, British paramountcy established
UPSC trap: Matching specific Governors-General, treaties, and territorial outcomes across all three wars in a single comparative question

concepts.name: British Acquisition of Delhi and Mughal Emperor's Protectorate (1803)
key_dimensions: Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon: Scindia's defeat transfers Delhi and Mughal Emperor to British 'protection'
Shah Alam II: blind, powerless emperor whose protector shifted from Maratha to British hands
Strategic significance: British now controlled the symbolic seat of Mughal sovereignty
UPSC trap: The Mughal Emperor did not become a British pensioner in 1803 — he remained nominal emperor until 1857; the nature of 'protection' must be precisely understood

concepts.name: Pindaris: Identity, Structure, and Their Role as Proximate Cause of the Third War
key_dimensions: Who were Pindaris: irregular horsemen, neither a caste nor a tribe — recruited from various communities, attached to Maratha armies
Their method of plunder and the British civilian complaints that forced Lord Hastings to act
Maratha chiefs' (Scindia, Holkar) informal patronage of Pindaris and British demand for disavowal
UPSC trap: Pindaris are often confused with Thuggee suppression (1830s) — different era, different nature, different British response mechanism
